topic: Reproducing a program
lesson: Matching a reference program to 5e-13 Eh means reproducing its constants, not only its equations: xtb 6.7.1's older bohr constant moves energies by up to 1e-07 Eh and its single-precision literals by 6e-10 Eh, more than a loose comparison would ever show. A second, independent implementation (tblite) separated program quirks from the method's definition.

topic: Different answers are not always bugs
lesson: Open-shell metal clusters at low electronic temperature and one test structure have several self-consistent solutions. Restarting each program from the other's converged moments shows whether a mismatch is a second solution of the same equations or an implementation error; every mismatch in the matrix was settled this way.

topic: Cheap invariance tests find real bugs
lesson: Permuting the atoms of CsOH changed xtb's and tblite's ALPB energy by 2.9e-03 Eh. That one test led to the Born-radius bug, and reading the same routine found the reference-state error.

topic: Input validation
lesson: xtb and tblite return energies for impossible electron counts, with atomic charges that do not add up to the molecular charge. A wrapper cannot see this from the energy alone; axtb checks electron counts before and after filling the orbitals.

topic: Threads
lesson: With OpenMP left to its defaults, a batch of 1024 xtb jobs on 128 workers took 30.6 s on the 64-core node instead of 1.0 s with one thread per job. axtb has no implicit threading, so there is no setting to forget.

topic: Start-up dominates small molecules
lesson: A water energy and gradient takes 0.7 ms of calculation inside an axtb process, 1.8 ms for the whole process, and 15 ms for the xtb 6.8.0 program (laptop, one thread). For small molecules, how a calculation is started matters more than how fast its code is.

topic: Math libraries depend on the CPU
lesson: For the generalized eigenproblem at n = 1000 on the Intel laptop, Intel MKL was the fastest library at 1, 4 and 8 threads. With 64 single-thread processes on the AMD Zen 5 node, Intel MKL was the slowest (1.19–1.31× faer's time) and AMD AOCL the fastest at n = 266. A library choice measured on one CPU does not carry over to another.

topic: SMT
lesson: 128 single-thread eigensolver processes on the 64-core node each ran about 1.9× slower than 64, so filling the SMT threads changed linear-algebra throughput by a factor of 1.04–1.06.

topic: Analytic Hessians are more accurate, not only faster
lesson: Against a tightly converged reference the analytic Hessian's frequencies were within 6e-05 cm⁻¹ for every test system; finite differences at their default settings were off by up to 0.7 cm⁻¹ in the gas phase, from the SCF convergence of each displacement. With implicit solvent it is worse (14 cm⁻¹ in the soft modes of caffeine): the ALPB/GBSA surface term is smooth in its first derivatives but not its second, so a finite-difference Hessian depends on the step, while the analytic one is the exact derivative at the point. For transition-state searches, where the imaginary and low modes decide the outcome, this matters as much as the speed.

topic: xtb --hess ignored --acc for GFN2-xTB
lesson: xtb 6.7.1 runs the displacement SCFs of a GFN2-xTB Hessian at its own fixed SCC accuracy whatever --acc says; only $hess sccacc in an xcontrol file changes it. On caffeine its --hess --acc 0.001 is therefore 2.2e-04 Eh/bohr² from the analytic Hessian and $hess sccacc=0.001 3.7e-05, xtb's own finite-difference error. xtb 6.8.0 passes --acc to the displacements (PR #1500): 3.7e-05 at --acc 0.001.

topic: Process start-up on many-core machines
lesson: Two dependencies of faer (private-gemm-x86, gemm-common) read the CPU cache sizes by opening every cache file of every CPU in /sys: thousands of opens per process on a 128-thread node, which the kernel serializes when many processes start together. 1024 axtb CLI runs on 128 workers took 5.87 s as benchmarked, 5.74 s with axtb's own thread-pool fix alone, and 0.52 s once the scan read one CPU only. The laptop, with 16 threads, barely shows it.

topic: More threads can be slower
lesson: For the 999-atom water cluster on the node, faer's eigensolver took 2.19 s on 8 threads and 4.39 s on 64. Beyond about 8 threads a single calculation gets slower; on a big node, run many calculations with a few threads each.

topic: A better SCF converger is not a free win
lesson: On a hard-SCF set (bond breaking, path images, metal clusters, small gaps) DIIS cut failures from 20 to 10 (10 to 0 at 300 K; the 0 K failures have no stable whole-electron solution for any program). But in systems with several SCF solutions it sometimes lands on a different one, once with an implausible −3 charge on an atom, and it lost one structure the reference mixer converges. So axtb keeps the reference mixer and uses DIIS only as a fallback: nothing that converges today changes, and rescued results are labelled.

topic: Defaults can be badly wrong, and only an independent implementation shows it
lesson: The g-xTB 2.0.1 program's Hessian at its default accuracy puts taxol's frequencies up to 149 cm⁻¹ off. Nothing in its output warns; it took an independent analytic Hessian, checked against tight references, to see it. The common tighter setting (--acc 0.001) keeps the error at 1.1 cm⁻¹, but a check on a single small molecule would have suggested that the default was safe.

topic: A complete specification makes reimplementation fast
lesson: Once every g-xTB 2.0.1 term had been decoded and each had captured reference values, the implementation took a few hours of agent time: 84 molecules across H–Lr reproduce the program to 9.1e-12 Eh with identical SCF iteration counts. Decoding was the slow part; writing the code against per-term reference numbers was not.

topic: The published derivation is not the program
lesson: For g-xTB v1.1, the paper's supporting information and the released program disagree in about ten places. Reproducing a method's published numbers means following the program; the supporting information is best read as intent.

topic: GPUs without fast FP64
lesson: At 6000 basis functions the RTX PRO 6000 eigensolver made a whole calculation 2.5× faster than the node's best CPU run in FP64 and 3.6× with adaptive precision. Mixed precision helps less than the FP32/FP64 rate gap suggests, because its FP64 refinement steps are matrix multiplies at the card's low FP64 rate.

topic: The retry temperature is part of the result
lesson: A common retry ladder reruns a failed GFN2 solvation pair at a higher electronic temperature. For HF stretched to 3 Å the pair converged only at 5000 K, after 47 s of failing 1000-iteration attempts; axtb's default converger finishes it at 300 K in 0.1 s, and the solvation correction then differs by 0.029 Eh (18 kcal/mol). Which rung converged changes the energy, so a path profile mixing rungs is not one surface; record the rung with every result.

topic: Comparing orbitals across programs needs overlaps, not coefficients
lesson: xtb, tblite and g-xTB 1.1.0 each write Molden files with their own normalization and ordering, so coefficients cannot be compared directly. Reading every file with an independent reader and comparing orbitals through the overlap of the two bases (1 − |⟨i|i⟩|, degenerate sets by singular values) showed agreement to 1e-09 or better per orbital (g-xTB 1.1.0's UF₆ apart, where the two SCFs take different paths) and found the dialect differences on the way.

topic: Most of a thermochemistry difference can be atomic masses
lesson: On the same Hessian, axtb's default vibrational analysis and xtb's differ by up to 0.10 cm⁻¹ and 4.0e-06 Eh in G(RRHO) (caffeine), almost all from the hydrogen mass (1.0080 in current standard atomic weights, 1.00794 in xtb). With xtb's masses and projection the two agree to 1e-10 Eh.

topic: One array can set a program's size limit
lesson: xtb's GFN-FF needs 9.0 GiB for a 3000-atom water cluster and fails at 5100 atoms, almost all from one hydrogen-bond bookkeeping array that grows as N³. Building the same hydrogen-bond lists from neighbour lists, axtb's GFN-FF needs 190 MiB at 3000 atoms and 1.5 GiB at 9900, with identical energies where both run. Its only dense array is the charge model's matrix, which now sets the time above a few thousand atoms.

topic: Differentiating code is not differentiating the formula
lesson: GFN-FF's bend, torsion and hydrogen-bond gradients are 0/0 at exactly linear or planar geometries; xtb guards them. Differentiating the literal guarded code gave Hessian errors of up to 0.15 Eh/bohr² for CO₂, hundreds of cm⁻¹ in its frequencies. The Hessian uses algebraically identical smooth forms, while energies and gradients keep xtb's exact operations, and finite differences at linear and planar test geometries confirm both.

topic: Bit-for-bit can mean the compiler's arithmetic
lesson: Some GFN-FF topology decisions in symmetric molecules are ties decided in the last bit of a vector norm. The Intel compilers inline NORM2 with different fused multiply-add orders, and xtb 6.7.1 (ifort) and 6.8.0 (ifx) round it differently, which decides which of several equidistant neighbours comes first. Matching each, read from the binary's disassembly, was needed to reproduce NF₃'s out-of-plane term and a nitrogen torsion list.

topic: Restarting the SCF saves iterations but can change the answer
lesson: Starting each SCF from the previous geometry's solution cut GFN2-xTB's iterations per point by 27%–42% along optimizations and random walks, g-xTB's by 3%–43% (an IRC from 9 to 5 per step). But a restart follows its own SCF solution: recompressing a stretched bond (N2 at 3000 K, F2) ended up to 0.32 Eh above a fresh start, metal clusters differed either way, and the programs do the same within one run. Paths through bond breaking should check against fresh starts. During development a restarted g-xTB SCF also stopped just at the thresholds with history-dependent gradient noise, which doubled a geomeTRIC optimization's steps until restarts converged ten times tighter.
